Hierarchy of Conservation Laws
of Diffusion–Convection Equations
Roman O. Popovych † and Nataliya M. Ivanova ‡
Institute of Mathematics of National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine,
3 Tereshchenkivska Str., Kyiv-4, 01601, Ukraine

E-mail: †rop@imath.kiev.ua, ‡ivanova@imath.kiev.ua

Abstract

We introduce notions of equivalence of conservation laws with respect to Lie symmetry groups for fixed systems of differential equations and with respect to equivalence groups or sets of admissible transformations for classes of such systems. We also revise the notion of linear dependence of conservation laws and define the notion of local dependence of potentials. To construct conservation laws, we develop and apply the most direct method which is effective to use in the case of two independent variables. Admitting possibility of dependence of conserved vectors on a number of potentials, we generalize the iteration procedure proposed by Bluman and Doran-Wu for finding nonlocal (potential) conservation laws. As an example, we completely classify potential conservation laws (including arbitrary order local ones) of diffusion–convection equations with respect to the equivalence group and construct an exhaustive list of locally inequivalent potential systems corresponding to these equations.

1 Introduction

After the Emmy Noether’s remarkable paper [29] had become well-known, a number of authors (see e.g. [30, 20, 37, 39]) searched for conservation laws using the symmetry approach based on the Noether’s results. In view of the generalized Noether’s theorem [30], there exists one-to-one correspondence between the non-trivial generalized variational symmetries of some functional and the non-trivial conservation laws of the associated Euler–Lagrange equations, and any such symmetry is a generalized symmetry of the Euler–Lagrange equations.

The Noether’s approach has a number of advantages. It reduces construction of conservation laws to finding symmetries for which there exist a number of well-developed methods, and complete description of necessary symmetry properties is known for a lot of systems of differential equations. However, this approach can be applied only to Euler–Lagrange equations that form normal systems and admit symmetry groups satisfying an additional “variational” property of leaving the variational integral invariant in some sense [30]. The latter requirements lead to restriction of class of systems that could be investigated in such way.

At the same time, the definition of conservation laws itself gives rise to a method of finding conservation laws. Technique of calculations used in the framework of this method is similar to the classical Lie method yielding symmetries of differential equations [19, Chapter 6]. As mentioned in the above reference, such algorithmic possibility was first employed by P.-S. Laplace [26] for derivation of the well-known Laplace vector of the two-body Kepler problem. Following tradition from group analysis of differential equations, we may call this method direct and distinguish four its versions, depending on the way of taking into account systems under investigation. (See e.g. [7, 3, 4, 22] and Section 4 of this paper for more details as well as [43] for comparison of the versions and their realizations in computer algebra programs.) In the present paper we use the most direct version based on immediate solving of determining equations for conserved vectors of conservations laws on the solution manifolds of investigated systems.

Let us note that there exist other approaches for construction of conservation laws which differ from the Noether’s or above direct ones, are based on exploitation of symmetry properties of differential equations and can be applied to non-Lagrangian systems. Thus, W.I. Fushchych and A.G. Nikitin [16] proposed to calculate directly bilinear combinations of solutions of motion equations, which are conserved in time by virtue of symmetries of these equations. It is possible in such way to find conservation laws corresponding to non-geometric symmetries. In the recent work [2] a purely algebraic formula has been derived for generating conservation laws of systems of differential equations that possess a scaling-invariance.

To classify conservation laws, instead of the usual equivalence relation on their set (more exactly, on the set of conserved vectors) we propose to use the natural and more general notions of equivalences of conservation laws with respect to Lie symmetry groups for fixed systems of differential equations and with respect to equivalence groups or sets of admissible point (or contact) transformations for classes of such systems. Results of classification up to these equivalences are more comprehensible, especially, if a whole class of systems is studied and blend with the framework of group analysis.

G. Bluman and P.R. Doran-Wu [7] proposed an ingenious procedure of branching iterations for finding nonlocal (potential) conservation laws of diffusion equations. Namely, on each iteration they use a conservation law from the previous iteration (one conservation law for one iteration) to introduce a potential and to construct the extended potential system. Then they study local conservation laws of the potential system, which are, generally speaking, nonlocal (potential) conservation laws for the initial equation. To the best of our knowledge, it was the first paper where the idea of hierarchy of potential systems and associated conservation laws is presented in an explicit form.

We generalize the iteration procedure by G. Bluman and P. Doran-Wu, admitting dependence of conserved vectors on different number (from one to the maximum possible that) of new potentials on each iteration. The idea of a similar approach was adduced in [42] and was formalized in the form of notion of universal Abelian covering of differential equations [41, 9, 35]. Such approach naturally results in the questions on some independence of employed potentials. That is why, in this paper we consider definition of linear dependence of conservation laws in detail and define the notion of local dependence of potentials.

Therefore, in the first part of the paper we propose some technique and discuss the classification problem for conservation laws in general. The ultimate goal of the second part is to present an exhaustive classification of potential conservation laws in a quite difficult and interesting case. As an illustration of the proposed technique, we choose the class of diffusion–convection equations

ut=(A⁡(u)​ux)x+B⁡(u)​ux,u_{t}=(A(u)u_{x})_{x}+B(u)u_{x}, (1)

where A=A⁡(u)A=A(u) and B=B⁡(u)B=B(u) are arbitrary smooth functions of uu, A⁡(u)≠0A(u)\!\neq\!0. Symmetry properties of (1) were considered in [12, 31, 44], however the complete and strong group classification of (1) was first presented in [33] (see also references therein for more details about symmetry analysis of classes intersecting class (1)).

Studying conservation laws of equations (1) was started from linear equations [37]. V.A. Dorodnitsyn and S.R. Svirshchevskii [11] (see also [19, Chapter 10]) completely investigated the local conservation laws for reaction–diffusion equations ut=(A⁡(u)​ux)x+C⁡(u)u_{t}=(A(u)u_{x})_{x}+C(u). The first-order local conservation laws of equations (1) were constructed by A.H. Kara and F.M. Mahomed [23]. Developing results of [7] obtained for the case B=0B=0, N.M. Ivanova [21] classified the first-order local conservation laws for equations (1) with respect to the equivalence group and constructed potential conservation laws of the first level. Namely, she made two steps of the iteration procedure, looking, in the second step, for the first-order local conservation laws of the potential systems obtained after the first step.

In the present work we exhaustively classify, with respect to the corresponding equivalence group, the local conservation laws of an arbitrary order, find the simplest and general potential conservation laws and construct locally inequivalent potential systems of equations (1). All possible steps of the branching iteration procedure are done, and admission of dependence of conserved vectors on a number of potentials is of fundamental importance for completing iterations. We obtain eight inequivalent cases of equations (1) having different sets of potential conservation laws:

  • •

    the general case (the parameter-functions AA and BB are arbitrary);

  • •

    three cases with an arbitrary value of AA and a special value of BB (B=0B=0; B=AB=A; B=∫A​𝑑u+u​AB=\int\!A\,du+uA);

  • •

    three corresponding linearizable equations (A=u−2A=u^{-2}, B=0B=0; A=B=u−2A=B=u^{-2}; A=1A=1, B=2​uB=2u) and

  • •

    the linear heat equation (A=1A=1, B=0B=0).

The latter case takes on special significance in our consideration since investigation of the linearizable equations having infinite series of potential conservation laws is reduced to this case and the non-linearizable equations from class (1) have at the most two independent conservation laws.

Our paper is organized as follows. First of all (Section 2) we give a basic theoretical background, following the spirit of [30]. We recall the notions of equivalence of conserved vectors and characteristics with respect to the triviality relation and discuss properties of the space of conserved vectors and the space of characteristics. This naturally results in the notions of linear dependence of conservation laws and local dependence of potentials (Sections 4 and 5).

In Section 3 we introduce the notions of equivalence of conservation laws with respect to Lie symmetry groups for fixed systems of differential equations and equivalence groups or sets of admissible point (or contact) transformations for classes of such systems. We emphasize possibility of solving classification problems for conservation laws with respect to the above equivalences similarly to usual group classification problems for differential equations.

In Section 4 we adduce different versions of the direct method of construction of conservation laws, emphasizing the most direct one and combining it with classification up to symmetry or equivalence groups. We also generalize the iteration method of finding potential conservation laws and associated potential systems.

Since the two-dimensional case is special for construction of potential systems we describe it in more detail in Section 5.

Then we apply the theoretical background given in the previous sections to investigation of diffusion–convection equations from class (1). The local conservation laws of (1) are classified with respect to the corresponding equivalence group in Section 6. In Section 7 we construct simplest potential conservation laws and analyze connections between them using potential equivalence transformations. The subject of Section 8 is the description of general potential conservation laws of the linear heat equation. In Section 9 we complete studying potential conservation laws of diffusion–convection equations and adduce the hierarchy of conservation laws obtained in our framework. In the same section we give an exhaustive list of locally inequivalent potential systems of equations (1). The obtained results can be interpreted as construction of universal Abelian covering for the whole class of diffusion–convection equations.

2 Basic definitions and statements

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be a system L⁡(x,u(ρ))=0L(x,u_{(\rho)})=0 of ll differential equations L1=0L^{1}=0, …, Ll=0L^{l}=0 for mm unknown functions u=(u1,…,um)u=(u^{1},\ldots,u^{m}) of nn independent variables x=(x1,…,xn).x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}). Here u(ρ)u_{(\rho)} denotes the set of all the derivatives of the functions uu with respect to xx of order no greater than ρ\rho, including uu as the derivatives of the zero order. Let ℒ(k)\mathcal{L}_{(k)} denote the set of all algebraically independent differential consequences that have, as differential equations, orders no greater than kk. We identify ℒ(k)\mathcal{L}_{(k)} with the manifold determined by ℒ(k)\mathcal{L}_{(k)} in the jet space J(k)J^{(k)}.

Definition 1.

A conservation law of the system ℒ\mathcal{L} is a divergence expression Div​F:=Di​Fi{\rm Div}\,F:=D_{i}F^{i} which vanishes for all solutions of ℒ\mathcal{L}: Div​F|ℒ=0.{\rm Div}F\bigl|_{\mathcal{L}}=0. The nn-tuple F=(F1​(x,u(r)),…,Fn​(x,u(r)))F=(F^{1}(x,u_{(r)}),\ldots,F^{n}(x,u_{(r)})) is called a conserved vector of this (local) conservation law.

In Definition 1 and below Di=DxiD_{i}=D_{x_{i}} denotes the operator of total differentiation with respect to the variable xix_{i}, i.e. Di=∂xi+uaα,i∂uαaD_{i}=\partial_{x_{i}}+u^{a}_{\alpha,i}\partial_{u^{a}_{\alpha}}, where uαau^{a}_{\alpha} and uα,iau^{a}_{\alpha,i} stand for the variables in jet spaces, which correspond to derivatives ∂|α|ua/∂x1α1​…​∂xnαn\partial^{|\alpha|}u^{a}/\partial x_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\ldots\partial x_{n}^{\alpha_{n}} and ∂uαa/∂xi\partial u^{a}_{\alpha}/\partial x_{i}, α=(α1,…,αn)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}), αi∈ℕ∪{0}\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, |α|:=α1+⋯+αn|\alpha|{:}=\alpha_{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{n}. We use the summation convention for repeated indices and assume any function as its zero-order derivative. The notation V|ℒV\bigl|_{\mathcal{L}} means that values of VV are considered only on solutions of the system ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Definition 2.

A conserved vector FF is called trivial if Fi=F^i+Fˇi,i=1,n¯,F^{i}=\hat{F}^{i}+\check{F}^{i},\quad i=\overline{1,n}, where F^i\hat{F}^{i} and Fˇi\check{F}^{i} are, likewise FiF^{i}, functions of xx and derivatives of uu (i.e. differential functions), F^i\hat{F}^{i} vanish on the solutions of ℒ\mathcal{L} and the nn-tuple Fˇ=(Fˇ1,…,Fˇn)\check{F}=(\check{F}^{1},\ldots,\check{F}^{n}) is a null divergence (i.e. its divergence vanishes identically).

The triviality concerning the vanishing conserved vectors on solutions of the system can be easily eliminated by confining on the manifold of the system, taking into account all its necessary differential consequences.

A characterization of all null divergences is given by the following lemma (see e.g. [30]).

Lemma 1.

The nn-tuple F=(F1,…,Fn)F=(F^{1},\ldots,F^{n}), n≥2n\geq 2, is a null divergence (DivF≡0\mathop{\rm Div}\nolimits F\equiv 0) iff there exist smooth functions vi​jv^{ij} (i,j=1,n¯i,j=\overline{1,n}) of xx and derivatives of uu, such that vi​j=−vj​iv^{ij}=-v^{ji} and Fi=Dj​vi​jF^{i}=D_{j}v^{ij}.

The functions vi​jv^{ij} are called potentials corresponding to the null divergence FF. If n=1n=1 any null divergence is constant.

Definition 3.

Two conserved vectors FF and F′F^{\prime} are called equivalent if the vector-function F′−FF^{\prime}-F is a trivial conserved vector.

Note 1.

Sometimes other definitions of equivalence of conservation laws are used [15].

By the latter definition any trivial conserved vector is equivalent to the vanishing one. For any system ℒ\mathcal{L} of differential equations the set CV(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) of conserved vectors of its conservation laws is a linear space, and the subset CV0(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits_{0}(\mathcal{L}) of trivial conserved vectors is a linear subspace in CV(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}). The factor space CL(ℒ)=CV(ℒ)/CV0(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L})=\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L})/\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits_{0}(\mathcal{L}) coincides with the set of equivalence classes of CV(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) with respect to the equivalence relation adduced in Definition 3. We can identify elements of CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) with conservation laws and call CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) also as the space of conservation laws of ℒ\mathcal{L} (see e.g. [45]). That is why we assume description of the set of conservation laws as finding CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) that is equivalent to construction of either a basis if dimCL⁡(ℒ)<∞\dim\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L})<\infty or a system of generatrices in the infinite dimensional case, and we will additionally identify elements from CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) with their representatives in CV(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}). In contrast to the order rFr_{F} of a conserved vector FF as the maximal order of derivatives explicitly appearing in FF, the order of a conservation law as an element ℱ\cal F from CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) is called min⁡{rF|F∈CV(ℒ)​corresponds to​ℱ}\min\{r_{F}\,|\,F\in\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L})\ \mbox{corresponds to}\ {\cal F}\}. Under linear dependence of conservation laws we understand linear dependence of corresponding elements in CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}).

Definition 4.

Conservation laws of a system ℒ\mathcal{L} are called linearly dependent if there exists their linear combination having a trivial conserved vector.

Let the system ℒ\cal L be totally nondegenerate [30]. Then application of the Hadamard lemma to the definition of conservation law and integrating by parts imply that the left side of any conservation law of ℒ\mathcal{L} can be always presented up to the equivalence relation as a linear combination of left side of independent equations from ℒ\mathcal{L} with coefficients λμ\lambda^{\mu} being functions on a suitable jet space J(k)J^{(k)}:

DivF=λμ​Lμ.\mathop{\rm Div}\nolimits F=\lambda^{\mu}L^{\mu}. (2)

Here the order kk is determined by ℒ\mathcal{L} and the allowable order of conservation laws, μ=1,l¯\mu=\overline{1,l}.

Definition 5.

Formula (2) and the ll-tuple λ=(λ1,…,λl)\lambda=(\lambda^{1},\ldots,\lambda^{l}) are called the characteristic form and the characteristic of the conservation law DivF=0\mathop{\rm Div}\nolimits F=0 correspondingly.

The characteristic λ\lambda is trivial if it vanishes for all solutions of ℒ\cal L. Since ℒ\cal L is nondegenerate, the characteristics λ\lambda and λ~\tilde{\lambda} satisfy (2) for the same FF and, therefore, are called equivalent iff λ−λ~\lambda-\tilde{\lambda} is a trivial characteristic. Similarly to conserved vectors, the set Ch(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) of characteristics corresponding to conservation laws of the system ℒ\cal L is a linear space, and the subset Ch0(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits_{0}(\mathcal{L}) of trivial characteristics is a linear subspace in Ch(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}). The factor space Chf(ℒ)=Ch(ℒ)/Ch0(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits_{\rm f}(\mathcal{L})=\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits(\mathcal{L})/\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits_{0}(\mathcal{L}) coincides with the set of equivalence classes of Ch(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) with respect to the above characteristic equivalence relation.

The following result [30] forms the cornerstone for the methods of studying conservation laws, which are based on formula (2), including the Noether theorem and the direct method by Anco and Bluman [3, 4].

Theorem 1 ([30]).

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be a normal, totally nondegenerate system of differential equations. Then representation of conservation laws of ℒ\mathcal{L} in the characteristic form (2) generates a one-to-one linear mapping between CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) and Chf(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits_{\rm f}(\mathcal{L}).

Using properties of total divergences, we can exclude the conserved vector FF from (2) and obtain a condition for the characteristic λ\lambda only. Namely, a differential function ff is a total divergence, i.e. f=DivFf=\mathop{\rm Div}F for some nn-tuple FF of differential functions iff 𝖤(f)=0\mathop{\sf E}(f)=0. Hereafter the Euler operator 𝖤=(𝖤1,…,𝖤m)\mathop{\sf E}=(\mathop{\sf E}^{1},\ldots,\mathop{\sf E}^{m}) is the mm-tuple of differential operators

𝖤a=(−D)α∂uαa,a=1,m¯,{\mathop{\sf E}}^{a}=(-D)^{\alpha}\partial_{u^{a}_{\alpha}},\quad a=\overline{1,m},

where α=(α1,…,αn)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}) runs the multi-indices set (αi∈ℕ∪{0}\alpha_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}), (−D)α=(−D1)α1​…​(−Dm)αm(-D)^{\alpha}=(-D_{1})^{\alpha_{1}}\ldots(-D_{m})^{\alpha_{m}}. Therefore, action of the Euler operator on (2) results to the equation

𝖤(λμ​Lμ)=𝖣λ∗(L)+𝖣L∗(λ)=0,\mathop{\sf E}(\lambda^{\mu}L^{\mu})={\mathop{\sf D}}_{\lambda}^{*}(L)+{\mathop{\sf D}}_{L}^{*}(\lambda)=0, (3)

which is a necessary and sufficient condition on characteristics of conservation laws for the system ℒ\mathcal{L}. The matrix differential operators 𝖣λ∗{\mathop{\sf D}}_{\lambda}^{*} and 𝖣L∗{\mathop{\sf D}}_{L}^{*} are the adjoints of the Fréchet derivatives 𝖣λ{\mathop{\sf D}}_{\lambda}^{\phantom{*}} and 𝖣L{\mathop{\sf D}}_{L}^{\phantom{*}}, i.e.

𝖣λ∗(L)=((−D)α​(∂λμ∂uαa​Lμ)),𝖣L∗(λ)=((−D)α​(∂Lμ∂uαa​λμ)).{\mathop{\sf D}}_{\lambda}^{*}(L)=\left((-D)^{\alpha}\left(\dfrac{\partial\lambda^{\mu}}{\partial u^{a}_{\alpha}}L^{\mu}\right)\right),\qquad{\mathop{\sf D}}_{L}^{*}(\lambda)=\left((-D)^{\alpha}\left(\dfrac{\partial L^{\mu}}{\partial u^{a}_{\alpha}}\lambda^{\mu}\right)\right).

Since 𝖣λ∗(L)=0{\mathop{\sf D}}_{\lambda}^{*}(L)=0 automatically on solutions of ℒ\mathcal{L} then equation (3) implies a necessary condition for λ\lambda to belong to Ch(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}):

𝖣L∗(λ)|ℒ=0.{\mathop{\sf D}}_{L}^{*}(\lambda)\bigl|_{\mathcal{L}}=0. (4)

Condition (4) can be considered as adjoint to the criteria 𝖣L(η)|ℒ=0{\mathop{\sf D}}_{L}^{\phantom{*}}(\eta)\bigl|_{\mathcal{L}}=0 for infinitesimal invariance of ℒ\mathcal{L} with respect to evolutionary vector field having the characteristic η=(η1,…,ηm)\eta=(\eta^{1},\ldots,\eta^{m}). That is why solutions of (4) are called sometimes as cosymmetries [35, 6] or adjoint symmetries [4].

3 Equivalence of conservation laws

We can essentially simplify and order classification of conservation laws, taking into account additionally symmetry transformations of a system or equivalence transformations of a whole class of systems. Such problem is similar to one of group classification of differential equations.

Proposition 1.

Any point transformation gg maps a class of equations in the conserved form into itself. More exactly, the transformation gg: x~=xg​(x,u)\tilde{x}=x_{g}(x,u), u~=ug​(x,u)\tilde{u}=u_{g}(x,u) prolonged to the jet space J(r)J^{(r)} transforms the equation Di​Fi=0D_{i}F^{i}=0 to the equation Di​Fgi=0D_{i}F^{i}_{g}=0. The transformed conserved vector FgF_{g} is determined by the formula

Fgi​(x~,u~(r))=Dxj​x~i|Dx​x~|​Fj​(x,u(r)),i.e.Fg​(x~,u~(r))=1|Dx​x~|​(Dx​x~)​F​(x,u(r))F_{g}^{i}(\tilde{x},\tilde{u}_{(r)})=\frac{D_{x_{j}}\tilde{x}_{i}}{|D_{x}\tilde{x}|}\,F^{j}(x,u_{(r)}),\quad\mbox{i.e.}\quad F_{g}(\tilde{x},\tilde{u}_{(r)})=\frac{1}{|D_{x}\tilde{x}|}(D_{x}\tilde{x})F(x,u_{(r)}) (5)

in the matrix notions. Here |Dx​x~||D_{x}\tilde{x}| is the determinant of the matrix Dx​x~=(Dxj​x~i)D_{x}\tilde{x}=(D_{x_{j}}\tilde{x}_{i}).

Note 2.

In the case of one dependent variable (m=1m=1) gg can be a contact transformation: x~=xg​(x,u(1))\tilde{x}=x_{g}(x,u_{(1)}), u~(1)=ug⁡(1)​(x,u(1))\tilde{u}_{(1)}=u_{g(1)}(x,u_{(1)}). Similar notes are also true for the statements below.

Definition 6.

Let GG be a symmetry group of the system ℒ\mathcal{L}. Two conservation laws with the conserved vectors FF and F′F^{\prime} are called GG-equivalent if there exists a transformation g∈Gg\in G such that the conserved vectors FgF_{g} and F′F^{\prime} are equivalent in the sense of Definition 3.

Any transformation g∈Gg\in G induces a linear one-to-one mapping g∗g_{*} in CV(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}), transforms trivial conserved vectors only to trivial ones (i.e. CV0(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits_{0}(\mathcal{L}) is invariant with respect to g∗g_{*}) and therefore induces a linear one-to-one mapping gfg_{\rm f} in CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}). It is obvious that gfg_{\rm f} preserves linear (in)dependence of elements in CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) and maps a basis (a set of generatrices) of CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) in a basis (a set of generatrices) of the same space. In such way we can consider the GG-equivalence relation of conservation laws as well-determined on CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) and use it to classify conservation laws.

Proposition 2.

If the system ℒ\mathcal{L} admits a one-parameter group of transformations then the infinitesimal generator X=ξi∂i+ηa∂uaX=\xi^{i}\partial_{i}+\eta^{a}\partial_{u^{a}} of this group can be used for construction of new conservation laws from known ones. Namely, differentiating equation (5) with respect to the parameter ε\varepsilon and taking the value ε=0\varepsilon=0, we obtain the new conserved vector

F~i=−X(r)​Fi+(Dj​ξi)​Fj−(Dj​ξj)​Fi.\widetilde{F}^{i}=-X_{(r)}F^{i}+(D_{j}\xi^{i})F^{j}-(D_{j}\xi^{j})F^{i}. (6)

Here X(r)X_{(r)} denotes the rr-th prolongation [30, 32] of the operator XX.

Note 3.

Formula (6) can be directly extended to generalized symmetry operators (see, for example, [5, 23]). A similar statement for generalized symmetry operators in evolutionary form (ξi=0\xi^{i}=0) was known earlier [18, 30]. It was used in [24] to introduce a notion of basis of conservation laws as a set which generates a whole set of conservation laws with action of generalized symmetry operators and operation of linear combination.

Proposition 3.

Any point transformation gg between systems ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}} induces a linear one-to-one mapping g∗g_{*} from CV(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) into CV(ℒ~)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}), which maps CV0(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits_{0}(\mathcal{L}) into CV0(ℒ~)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits_{0}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}) and generates a linear one-to-one mapping gfg_{\rm f} from CL(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}) into CL(ℒ~)\mathop{\rm CL}\nolimits(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}).

Corollary 1.

Any point transformation gg between systems ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}} induces a linear one-to-one mapping g^f\hat{g}_{\rm f} from Chf(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits_{\rm f}(\mathcal{L}) into Chf(ℒ~)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits_{\rm f}(\tilde{\mathcal{L}}).

It is possible to obtain an explicit formula for correspondence between characteristics of ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}}. Let ℒ~μ=Λμ​ν​ℒν\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{\mu}=\Lambda^{\mu\nu}\mathcal{L}^{\nu}, where Λμ​ν=Λμ​ν​α​Dα\Lambda^{\mu\nu}=\Lambda^{\mu\nu\alpha}D^{\alpha}, Λμ​ν​α\Lambda^{\mu\nu\alpha} are differential functions, α=(α1,…,αn)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}) runs the multi-indices set (αi∈ℕ∪{0}\alpha_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}), μ,ν=1,l¯\mu,\nu=\overline{1,l}. Then

λμ=Λν​μ∗​(|Dx​x~|​λ~ν).\lambda^{\mu}={\Lambda^{\nu\mu}}^{*}(|D_{x}\tilde{x}|\tilde{\lambda}^{\nu}).

Here Λν​μ∗=(−D)α⋅Λμ​ν​α{\Lambda^{\nu\mu}}^{*}=(-D)^{\alpha}\cdot\Lambda^{\mu\nu\alpha} is the adjoint to the operator Λν​μ\Lambda^{\nu\mu}. For a number of cases, e.g. if ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}} are single partial differential equations (l=1l=1), the operators Λμ​ν\Lambda^{\mu\nu} are simply differential functions (i.e. Λμ​ν​α=0\Lambda^{\mu\nu\alpha}=0 for |α|>0|\alpha|>0) and, therefore, Λν​μ∗=Λμ​ν{\Lambda^{\nu\mu}}^{*}=\Lambda^{\mu\nu}.

Consider the class ℒ|S\mathcal{L}|_{S} of systems L⁡(x,u(ρ),θ⁡(x,u(ρ)))=0L(x,u_{(\rho)},\theta(x,u_{(\rho)}))=0 parameterized with the parameter-functions θ=θ⁡(x,u(ρ)).\theta=\theta(x,u_{(\rho)}). Here LL is a tuple of fixed functions of x,x, u(ρ)u_{(\rho)} and θ.\theta. θ\theta denotes the tuple of arbitrary (parametric) functions θ⁡(x,u(ρ))=(θ1​(x,u(ρ)),…,θk​(x,u(ρ)))\theta(x,u_{(\rho)})=(\theta^{1}(x,u_{(\rho)}),\ldots,\theta^{k}(x,u_{(\rho)})) satisfying the condition S⁡(x,u(ρ),θ(q)​(x,u(ρ)))=0S(x,u_{(\rho)},\theta_{(q)}(x,u_{(\rho)}))=0. This condition consists of differential equations on θ\theta, where xx and u(ρ)u_{(\rho)} play the role of independent variables and θ(q)\theta_{(q)} stands for the set of all the partial derivatives of θ\theta of order no greater than qq. In what follows we call the functions θ\theta arbitrary elements. Denote the local transformations group preserving the form of systems from ℒ|S\mathcal{L}|_{S} as G∼=G∼​(L,S).G^{\mathop{\sim}}=G^{\mathop{\sim}}(L,S).

Consider the set P=P⁡(L,S)P=P(L,S) of all pairs each of which consists of a system from ℒ|S\mathcal{L}|_{S} and a conservation law of this system. In view of Proposition 3, action of transformations from G∼G^{\mathop{\sim}} together with the pure equivalence relation of conserved vectors naturally generates an equivalence relation on PP. Classification of conservation laws with respect to G∼G^{\mathop{\sim}} will be understood as classification in PP with respect to the above equivalence relation. This problem can be investigated in the way that is similar to group classification in classes of systems of differential equations. Namely, we construct firstly the conservation laws that are defined for all values of the arbitrary elements. (The corresponding conserved vectors may depend on the arbitrary elements.) Then we classify, with respect to the equivalence group, arbitrary elements for each of that the system admits additional conservation laws.

In an analogues way we also can introduce an equivalence relation on PP generated by all admissible point or contact transformations (called also form-preserving ones [25]) in pairs of equations from ℒ|S\mathcal{L}|_{S}.

Note 4.

It can be easy shown that all the above equivalences are indeed equivalence relations.

4 Direct iteration method of finding conservation laws

To construct conservation laws of a system ℒ\mathcal{L} of differential equations, we iterate a modification of the most direct method based on Definition 1. More precisely, the algorithm is as follows.

Zeroth iteration. At first we construct local conservation laws of ℒ\mathcal{L}. We fix an (arbitrary) order rr of conserved vectors under consideration. Then we introduce local coordinates (“unconstrained variables”) on the manifold ℒ(r+1){\mathcal{L}}_{(r+1)} determined by the system ℒ\mathcal{L} and its differential consequences in J(r+1)J^{(r+1)}. The other (“constrained”) variables of J(r+1)J^{(r+1)} are expressed via unconstrained ones by means of using the equations of ℒ(r+1){\mathcal{L}}_{(r+1)}. We substitute the expressions for constrained variables into a conservation law and split the obtained condition with respect to the unconstrained variables. This procedure results in a first-order linear system of determining equations for conserved vectors. Solving the determining equations up to the usual equivalence relation on CV(ℒ)\mathop{\rm CV}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}), we obtain complete description of local conservation laws of ℒ\mathcal{L}. To classify conservation laws in easier and more systematic way (especially for classes of systems of differential equations), instead of usual equivalence we use the introduced above equivalence with respect to symmetry or equivalence transformations. (See Section 6 for examples.)

First iteration. After applying Lemma 1 to constructed conservation laws on the set of solutions of ℒ=ℒ0\mathcal{L}={\mathcal{L}}^{0}, we introduce potentials as additional dependent variables and attach the equations connecting the potentials with components of corresponding conserved vectors to ℒ0{\mathcal{L}}^{0}. (If n>2n>2 the attached equations of such kind form an underdetermined system with respect to the potentials. Therefore, we can also attach gauge conditions on the potentials to ℒ0{\mathcal{L}}^{0}.)

We have to use linear independent conservation laws since otherwise the introduced potentials will be dependent in the following sense: there exists a linear combination of the potential tuples, which is, for some r′∈ℕr^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{N}}, a tuple of functions of xx and u(r′)u_{(r^{\prime})} only.

Then we exclude the unnecessary equations (i.e. the equations that are dependent on equations of ℒ0{\mathcal{L}}^{0} and attached equations simultaneously) from the extended (potential) system ℒ1{\mathcal{L}}^{1} which will be called a potential system of the first level. Any conservation law of ℒ0{\mathcal{L}}^{0} is a one of ℒ1{\mathcal{L}}^{1}. We iterate the above procedure of the direct method for ℒ1{\mathcal{L}}^{1} to find its conservation laws which are linear independent with ones from the previous iteration and will be called potential conservation laws of the first level.

Further iterations. We make iterations while it is possible (i.e. the iteration procedure has to be stopped if all the conservation laws of a potential system ℒk+1{\mathcal{L}}^{k+1} of the (k+1)(k+1)-th level are linear dependent with the ones of ℒk{\mathcal{L}}^{k}) or construct infinite chains of conservation laws by means of induction. This process may yield purely potential conservation laws of the initial system ℒ\mathcal{L}, which are linear independent with local conservation laws and, therefore, depend explicitly on potential variables.

Any conservation law from the previous step of iteration procedure will be a conservation law for the next step and vice versa, conservation laws which are obtained on the next step and depend only on variables of the previous step are linear dependent with conservation laws from the previous step. It is also obvious that the conservation laws used for construction of a potential system of the next level are trivial on the manifold of this system.

Since gauge conditions on potentials can be chosen in many different ways, exhaustive realization of iterations is improbable in the case n>2n>2.

The procedure of exclusion of constrained variables (which are described above in detail only for the zeroth iteration) is called in classical group analysis as “confining to the manifold of ℒ\mathcal{L}”. Taking into account ℒ\mathcal{L} in the above way, we automatically eliminate the ambiguity connected with vanishing conserved vectors on the solutions of ℒ\mathcal{L}. However, the second kind ambiguity arising via existence of null divergences is preserved, and it is the main reason of difficulties in realization of this algorithm with symbolic computation systems [43].

To find conservation laws on each step of iteration procedure, one can apply other methods which are based on the characteristic form (2) or its consequences (3) and (4). These methods are also called as direct [3, 4]. Following [43], for convenience we will numerate them as the second, third and fourth versions of the direct method in contrast to the above first one. They are close to the symmetry group method by Noether since in the case of Euler–Lagrange equations the coefficients λa\lambda^{a} are nothing else than Noether’s characteristics. Taking into account the equivalence relation on Ch(ℒ)\mathop{\rm Ch}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}), one can assume during calculations that characteristics depend only on unconstrained variables.

In the second version of the direct method the representation (2) is regarded as an equation defined on an open subset of J(k)J^{(k)} with respect to conserved vectors and characteristics simultaneously.

In the framework of the third version, sought quantities are characteristics only. Determining equation (3) is defined on an open subset of J(k)J^{(k)}. Conserved vectors are reconstructed from known characteristics via explicit integral formulas. An algorithm of this (third) version of the direct method was developed for Cauchy–Kovalevskaya systems by S. Anco and G. Bluman [3, 4] (see also [45, 30] for a theoretical background).

The fourth version is based on equation (4) which is defined on the manifold ℒ\mathcal{L} and is only a necessary condition on characteristic of conservation laws. Therefore, one has to choose characteristics from the set of adjoint symmetries using additional conditions. Such approach was used by G. Bluman and P. Doran-Wu [7] for studying conservation laws of diffusion equations.

Each from four above versions of the direct method has its advantages and disadvantages. A detailed comparative analysis of all the versions and their realizations in computer algebra programs are given by T. Wolf [43].

Prototypes and sources of a number of above ideas can be found in [27].

5 Two-dimensional case

The case of two independent variables is singular, in particular, with respect to possible (constant) indeterminacy after introduction of potentials and high effectiveness of application of potential symmetries. That is why we consider some notions connected with conservation laws in this case separately. We denote independent variables as tt (the time variable) and xx (the space one). Any local conservation law has the form

Dt​F​(t,x,u(r))+Dx​G​(t,x,u(r))=0.D_{t}F(t,x,u_{(r)})+D_{x}G(t,x,u_{(r)})=0. (7)

Here DtD_{t} and DxD_{x} are the operators of the total differentiation with respect to tt and xx. FF and GG are called the conserved density and the flux of the conservation law correspondingly.

Two conserved vectors (F,G)(F,G) and (F′,G′)(F^{\prime},G^{\prime}) are equivalent if there exist such functions F^\hat{F}, G^\hat{G} and HH of tt, xx and derivatives of uu that F^\hat{F} and G^\hat{G} vanish on ℒ(k)\mathcal{L}_{(k)} for some kk and

F′=F+F^+Dx​H,G′=G+G^−Dt​H.F^{\prime}=F+\hat{F}+D_{x}H,\qquad G^{\prime}=G+\hat{G}-D_{t}H. (8)

Any conservation law (7) of ℒ\mathcal{L} allows us to deduce the new dependent (potential) variable vv by means of the equations

vx=F,vt=−G.v_{x}=F,\qquad v_{t}=-G. (9)

To construct a number of potentials in one step, we have to use a set of linear independent conservation laws (see the previous section) since otherwise the potentials will be dependent in the following sense: there exists a linear combination of the potentials, which is, for some r′∈ℕr^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{N}}, a function of tt, xx and u(r′)u_{(r^{\prime})} only.

In the case of two independent variables we can also introduce the more general notion of potential dependence.

Definition 7.

The potentials v1v^{1}, …, vpv^{p} are called locally dependent on the set of solution of the system ℒ{\mathcal{L}} (or, briefly speaking, dependent) if there exist r′∈ℕr^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{N}} and a function HH of the variables tt, xx, u(r′)u_{(r^{\prime})}, v1v^{1}, …, vpv^{p} such that H⁡(t,x,u(r′),v1,…,vp)=0H(t,x,u_{(r^{\prime})},v^{1},\ldots,v^{p})=0 for any solution (u,v1,…,vp)(u,v^{1},\ldots,v^{p}) of the united system determining the set of potentials v1v^{1}, …, vpv^{p}.

Proof of local dependence or independence of potentials for general classes of differential equations is difficult since it is closely connected with precise description of possible structure of conservation laws. An example of such proof for diffusion–convection equations is presented below.

In the case of single equation ℒ\mathcal{L}, equations of form (9) combine into the complete potential system since ℒ\mathcal{L} is a differential consequence of (9). As a rule, systems of such kind admit a number of nontrivial symmetries and so they are of a great interest.

Equations (5) and (9) imply the following statement.

Proposition 4.

Any point transformation connecting two systems ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}} of PDEs with two independent variables generates a one-to-one mapping between the sets of potential systems, which correspond to ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ~\tilde{\mathcal{L}}. Generation is made via trivial prolongation on the space of introduced potential variables, i.e. we can assume that the potentials are not transformed.

Corollary 2.

The Lie symmetry group of a system ℒ\mathcal{L} of differential equations generates an equivalence group on the set of potential systems corresponding to ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Corollary 3.

Let ℒ^|S\widehat{\mathcal{L}}|_{S} be the set of all potential systems constructed for systems from the class ℒ|S\mathcal{L}|_{S} with their conservation laws. Action of transformations from G∼​(L,S)G^{\mathop{\sim}}(L,S) together with the equivalence relation of potentials naturally generates an equivalence relation on ℒ^|S\widehat{\mathcal{L}}|_{S}.

Note 5.

Proposition 4 and its Corollaries imply that the equivalence group for a class of systems or the symmetry group for single system can be prolonged to potential variables for any step of the direct iteration procedure. It is natural the prolonged equivalence groups are used to classify possible conservation laws and potential systems in each iteration. Additional equivalences which exist in some subclasses of the class or arise after introducing potential variables can be used for deeper analysis of connections between conservation laws.

If we know the precise structure of conservation laws the answer is almost obvious.

Theorem 5.

For any equation (1) potentials are locally dependent on the equation manifold iff the corresponding conservation laws are linear dependent.

Proof.

Since the direct statement of the theorem is obvious (see Section 5), we prove only the inverse statement, using the rule of contraries. Suppose that potentials v0v^{0}, …, vpv^{p} introduced with (independent) conservation laws of Cases 1–4 are locally dependent. The vanishing pp means local triviality of v0v^{0} as a potential, i.e. v0v^{0} can be expressed in terms of local variables and the corresponding conservation law is trivial. That is why it is sufficient to investigate only the special cases when the number of independent conservation laws is greater than 1. Therefore, p=1p=1 if either B=0B=0 or B=AB=A and p∈ℕ/{0}p\in\mathbb{N}/\{0\} for the linear heat equation.

Without loss of generality we can assume that there exist r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} and a fixed function VV of tt, xx, v¯=(v1,…​vp)\bar{v}=(v^{1},\ldots v^{p}) and u(r)u_{(r)} that v0=V⁡(t,x,v¯,u(r))v^{0}=V(t,x,\bar{v},u_{(r)}) for any solution of the united system determining the whole set of potentials v0v^{0}, …, vpv^{p}. Taking into account equation (1) and its differential consequences, we can assume that VV depends only on tt, xx, v¯\bar{v} and uk=∂ku/∂xku_{k}=\partial^{k}u/\partial x^{k}, k=0,r′¯,k=\overline{0,r^{\prime}}, where r′≤2​rr^{\prime}\leq 2r. Let us apply the operator DxD_{x} to the condition v0=V⁡(t,x,v¯,u,u1,…,ur′)v^{0}=V(t,x,\bar{v},u,u_{1},\ldots,u_{r^{\prime}}): vx0=Vx+Vvs​vxs+Vuk​uk+1v^{0}_{x}=V_{x}+V_{v^{s}}v^{s}_{x}+V_{u^{k}}u_{k+1}. (Hereafter the index ss takes the values from 1 to pp.) Since in any case under consideration vxs=fs​uv^{s}_{x}=f^{s}u for some functions fsf^{s} of tt and xx, we can split the differentiated condition with respect to uku_{k} step-by-step in the reverse sequence, beginning with the major derivative. As a result, we obtain Vuk=0V_{u^{k}}=0, Vx=0V_{x}=0 and f0=Vvs​fsf^{0}=V_{v^{s}}f^{s}, i.e. the functions f0f^{0}, …fpf^{p} are linear dependent. This gives a contradiction with the supposition that the conservation laws are independent. ∎

7 Simplest potential conservation laws
of diffusion–convection equations

Let us investigate local conservation laws of potential systems 1–4 from Table 1, which have the form

Dt​F​(t,x,u(r),v(r))+Dx​G​(t,x,u(r),v(r))=0.D_{t}F(t,x,u_{(r)},v_{(r)})+D_{x}G(t,x,u_{(r)},v_{(r)})=0. (17)

These laws can be considered as nonlocal (potential) conservation laws of equations from class (1). We assume them as simplest potential conservation laws since the corresponding potential systems are constructed from the initial equation (1) with one conservation law only.

We classify conservation laws up to the equivalence relation with respect to the transformation group Gpr∼G^{\mathop{\sim}}_{\rm pr} which is a result of the trivial prolongation of the group G∼G^{\mathop{\sim}} from Theorem 2 to the space of the potential vv.

Lemma 3.

Any conservation law of form (17) for each of systems 1–4 from Table 1 has the zero order, i.e. it is equivalent to a law with a conserved density FF and a flux GG that are independent on the (non-zero order) derivatives of uu and vv.

Proof.

Consider any from the systems 1–4. Taking it and its differential consequences into account, we can exclude dependence of FF and GG on the all (non-zero order) derivatives of vv and the derivatives of uu containing differentiation with respect to tt. The remain part of the proof is completely similar to the one of Lemma 2. ∎

In an analogous to Theorem 4 and more cumbersome way we prove the following statement.

t~=t,x~=v,v~=x,u~=u−1,A~=u−2​A,\tilde{t}=t,\quad\tilde{x}=v,\quad\tilde{v}=x,\quad\tilde{u}=u^{-1},\quad\tilde{A}=u^{-2}A, (27)

and the conservation law 1.3 is transformed to the local one of Case 3 where ε=0\varepsilon=0. The same transformation extended to the potential ww as w~=−w+v​ex\tilde{w}=-w+ve^{x} also reduces the potential system 1.3 to 1.2.

Linearizable equations. It is well known [8, 38, 14, 17, 10, 13, 40] that equations (1) G∼G^{\mathop{\sim}}-equivalent to ones of Cases 1.4, 1.5, 1.6 are linearized by a nonlocal (so-called potential equivalence [34, 28]) transformations to the linear heat equation. That is why these equations stand out against the other diffusion–convection equations with having an infinite number of linear independent purely potential conservation laws.

The u−2u^{-2}-diffusion equation ut=(u−2​ux)xu_{t}=(u^{-2}u_{x})_{x} is reduced to the linear heat equation [8] by the hodograph transformation (27). More exactly, (27) is a local transformation between the corresponding potential systems vx=uv_{x}=u, vt=u−2​uxv_{t}=u^{-2}u_{x} and vx=uv_{x}=u, vt=uxv_{t}=u_{x} constructed by means of using the “common” conservation law (Case 1). The u−2u^{-2}-diffusion equation has, as a subcase of the case B=0B=0, two linear independent local conservation laws with the conserved vectors

F1=u,G1=−u−2​ux,\displaystyle F^{1}=u,\quad G^{1}=-u^{-2}u_{x}, (28)
F2=x​u,G2=−x​u−2​ux−u−1\displaystyle F^{2}=xu,\quad G^{2}=-xu^{-2}u_{x}-u^{-1} (29)

(Cases 1 and 2 of Table 1) and the infinite series of potential conservation laws (Case 1.4) additionally. Under the action of hodograph transformation (27) the conservation law with conserved vector (28) is transformed to the trivial one of the linear heat equation with the conserved vector (1,0)(1,0). And vice versa, the conservation law of the linear heat equation corresponding to the value α=1\alpha=1 (Case 4) is transformed by (27) to the trivial one of the u−2u^{-2}-diffusion equation with the conserved vector (1,0)(1,0). The conservation law with conserved vector (29) is trivial on the manifold of potential system constructed by means of (28), is equivalent to the one from Case 1.4 with σ=1\sigma=1 and is transformed to Case 4.1, where α=1\alpha=1 and β=x\beta=x. Case 1.4 is reduced by (27) to Case 4, where α=σ\alpha=\sigma.

Since the equation ut=(u−2​ux)x+u−2​uxu_{t}=(u^{-2}u_{x})_{x}+u^{-2}u_{x} is reduced to the u−2u^{-2}-diffusion equation by the local transformation t~=t\tilde{t}=t, x~=ex\tilde{x}=e^{x}, u~=e−x​u\tilde{u}=e^{-x}u, its conservation laws are connected with ones of the linear heat equation in a way which is similar to the previous case.

The potential systems v~x~=u~\tilde{v}_{\tilde{x}}=\tilde{u}, v~t~=u~x~+u~2\tilde{v}_{\tilde{t}}=\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}+\tilde{u}^{2} and vx=uv_{x}=u, vt=uxv_{t}=u_{x} constructed with the “common” conservation law for the Burgers equation ut=ux​x+2​u​uxu_{t}=u_{xx}+2uu_{x} and the linear heat equation ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx} are connected via the transformation

t=t~,x=x~,u=u~​ev~,v=ev~.t=\tilde{t},\quad x=\tilde{x},\quad u=\tilde{u}e^{\tilde{v}},\quad v=e^{\tilde{v}}.

(Here the tilde variables correspond to the Burgers equation.) Let us note that really the famous Cole–Hopf transformation [10, 17] (first found in [14]) linearizes the Burgers equation to the “potential” heat equation vt=vx​xv_{t}=v_{xx} [28, 34]. The Burgers equation has the “common” local conservation law (Case 1) and the infinite series of simplest potential conservation laws (Case 1.6). The above transformation between the potential systems induces the one-to-one mapping preserving α\alpha between the infinite series 1.6 and the one 4 of the “potential” heat equation vt=vx​xv_{t}=v_{xx}. Then, the conservation law of form 4 with the function α~\tilde{\alpha} for the “potential” heat equation vt=vx​xv_{t}=v_{xx} is equivalent to the one with the function α\alpha for the heat equation ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx}, where α~=αx\tilde{\alpha}=\alpha_{x}. The conservation law of Case 1 for the Burgers equation is trivial on the manifold of the corresponding potential system and is mapped to trivial one of the system vx=uv_{x}=u, vt=uxv_{t}=u_{x}.

Linear heat equation. The linear heat equation ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx} has an infinite dimensional space of local conservation laws [11], which is generated by conserved vectors of the form

(Fα,Gα)=(α​u,αx​u−α​ux),(F^{\alpha},G^{\alpha})=(\alpha u,\alpha_{x}u-\alpha u_{x}),

where α=α⁡(t,x)\alpha=\alpha(t,x) is an arbitrary solution of the backward linear heat equation αt+αx​x=0\alpha_{t}+\alpha_{xx}=0. Using a fixed conservation law of such form, we can introduce the potential vαv^{\alpha}, where

vxα=α​u,vtα=α​ux−αx​u.v^{\alpha}_{x}=\alpha u,\quad v^{\alpha}_{t}=\alpha u_{x}-\alpha_{x}u. (30)

System (30) has one infinite series of conservation laws (Case 4.1) with conserved vectors

(Fα​β,Gα​β)=((βα)x​vα,−α​(βα)x​u−(βα)t​vα),(F^{\alpha\beta},G^{\alpha\beta})=\left(\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)_{x}v^{\alpha},-\alpha\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)_{x}\!u-\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)_{t}v^{\alpha}\right), (31)

where β=β⁡(t,x)\beta=\beta(t,x) is an arbitrary solution of the backward linear heat equation βt+βx​x=0\beta_{t}+\beta_{xx}=0. These conservation laws are simplest potential ones for the linear heat equation and allow us to introduce “second-level” potentials wα​βw^{\alpha\beta}. As a result, we obtain potential systems of the next level:

vxα=α​u,wxα​β=(βα)x​vα,wtα​β=α​(βα)x​u+(βα)t​vα.v^{\alpha}_{x}=\alpha u,\qquad w^{\alpha\beta}_{x}=\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)_{x}v^{\alpha},\qquad w^{\alpha\beta}_{t}=\alpha\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)_{x}\!u+\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)_{t}v^{\alpha}. (32)

Consider the system

vxα=α​u,vtα=α​ux−αx​u,vxβ=β​u,vtβ=β​ux−βx​uv^{\alpha}_{x}=\alpha u,\quad v^{\alpha}_{t}=\alpha u_{x}-\alpha_{x}u,\quad v^{\beta}_{x}=\beta u,\quad v^{\beta}_{t}=\beta u_{x}-\beta_{x}u (33)

that is the union of two potential systems of form (30) corresponding to the local conservation laws with the conserved vectors (Fα,Gα)(F^{\alpha},G^{\alpha}) and (Fβ,Gβ)(F^{\beta},G^{\beta}). In a similar way to the previous cases we can state that the second-level potential conservation law with conserved vector (31) is trivial on the solution manifold of system (33) since

Fα​β=Dx​(βα​vα−vβ)andGα​β=−Dt​(βα​vα−vβ).F^{\alpha\beta}=D_{x}\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}v^{\alpha}-v^{\beta}\right)\quad\mbox{and}\quad G^{\alpha\beta}=-D_{t}\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}v^{\alpha}-v^{\beta}\right).

Moreover, systems (32) and (33) are connected via the local substitution

wα​β=βα​vα−vβ.w^{\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}v^{\alpha}-v^{\beta}.

It implies that really system (33) is generated by only three independent equations. We can choose e.g. the equations

vxα=α​u,vxβ=β​u,βα​vtα−vtβ=α​(βα)x​u.v^{\alpha}_{x}=\alpha u,\quad v^{\beta}_{x}=\beta u,\quad\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}v^{\alpha}_{t}-v^{\beta}_{t}=\alpha\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)_{x}\!u.

As a result of our analysis, we can formulate the following statement.

Theorem 7.

For any non-linearized equation (1) and the linear heat equation the potential systems of the second level, which are constructed by means of using single conservation law of the simplest potential systems, are equivalent to first-level potential systems obtained with pairs of conservation laws.

8 Potential conservation laws of linear heat equation

With respect to G∼G^{\mathop{\sim}}-equivalence the linear heat equation is the unique linear equation in class (1). Investigation of its general potential conservation laws plays the major role in classification of potential conservation laws for linearizable equations in class (1) and, therefore, for whole class (1). (The simplest potential conservation laws are studied in the previous section.)

As proved in Theorem 4, the linear heat equation has the infinite series of local conservation laws. Fixing an arbitrary p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N} and choosing pp linear independent solutions α¯=(α1,…,αp)\bar{\alpha}=(\alpha^{1},\ldots,\alpha^{p}) of the backward linear heat equation, we obtain pp linear independent conservation laws with the conserved vectors (Fs,Gs)=(αs​u,αxs​u−αs​ux)(F^{s},G^{s})=(\alpha^{s}u,\alpha^{s}_{x}u-\alpha^{s}u_{x}). (Hereafter s=1,p¯s=\overline{1,p}.) In view of Theorem 5 the potentials v¯=(v1,…,vp)\bar{v}=(v^{1},\ldots,v^{p}) introduced with these conservation laws by the formulas

vxs=αs​u,vts=αs​ux−αxs​uv^{s}_{x}=\alpha^{s}u,\quad v^{s}_{t}=\alpha^{s}u_{x}-\alpha^{s}_{x}u (34)

are independent in the sense of Definition 7.

For the linear heat equation the complete set of first level potential conservation laws is indeed the union set of conservation laws of systems (34) corresponding to all possible values of pp and pp-tuples α¯\bar{\alpha}. The following theorem is true.

Theorem 8.

Any local conservation law of system (34) is equivalent on the manifold of system (34) to a local conservation law of the linear heat equation.

Corollary 4.

For the linear heat equation potential conservation laws of any level are equivalent to local ones on the manifolds of the corresponding potential systems, and potentials of any level are locally expressed via local variables tt, xx, u(r)u_{(r)} (for some rr) and potentials of the first level only.

We present the proof of Theorem 8 as the chain of simple and nice lemmas.

Lemma 4.

Any local conservation law of system (34) is equivalent to that with the conserved vector (K​u,Kx​u−K​ux)(Ku,K_{x}u-Ku_{x}) where the function K=K⁡(t,x,v¯)K=K(t,x,\bar{v}) is determined by the system

Kt+Kx​x=0,αs​Kx​vs−αxs​Kvs=0.K_{t}+K_{xx}=0,\qquad\alpha^{s}K_{xv^{s}}-\alpha^{s}_{x}K_{v^{s}}=0. (35)
Proof.

Consider a local conservation law of system (34) in the most general form, where the conserved vector is a vector-function of tt, xx and derivatives of the functions uu and vsv^{s} from the zero order up to some finite one. Taking into account system (34) and its differential consequences, we can exclude dependence of the conserved vector on the all (non-zero order) derivatives of vsv^{s} and the derivatives of uu containing differentiation with respect to tt. Similarly to Lemma 2 we can prove that the reduced conserved vector (F,G)(F,G) does not depend on (non-zero order) derivatives of uu and, moreover, F=F⁡(t,x,v¯)F=F(t,x,\bar{v}), G=−αs​Fvs​(t,x,v¯)​u+G0​(t,x,v¯)G=-\alpha^{s}F_{v^{s}}(t,x,\bar{v})u+G^{0}(t,x,\bar{v}). The function FF and G0G^{0} satisfy the system

αs​αs′​Fvs​vs′=0,αs​Gvs0=2​αxs​Fvs+αs​Fx​vs,Ft+Gx0=0.\alpha^{s}\alpha^{s^{\prime}}F_{v^{s}v^{s^{\prime}}}=0,\qquad\alpha^{s}G^{0}_{v^{s}}=2\alpha^{s}_{x}F_{v^{s}}+\alpha^{s}F_{xv^{s}},\qquad F_{t}+G^{0}_{x}=0.

Let us pass on to the equivalent conserved vector (F~,G~)(\widetilde{F},\widetilde{G}), where F~=F+Dx​H\widetilde{F}=F+D_{x}H, G~=G−Dt​H\widetilde{G}=G-D_{t}H and H=H⁡(t,x,v¯)H=H(t,x,\bar{v}) is a solution of the equations Hx=−FH_{x}=-F, Ht=GH_{t}=G. (The variables vsv^{s} is assumed as parameters in the latter equations.) Then F~=K​u\widetilde{F}=Ku, G~=Kx​u−K​ux\widetilde{G}=K_{x}u-Ku_{x}. The function K=αs​HvsK=\alpha^{s}H_{v^{s}} depends on tt, xx and v¯\bar{v} and satisfy system (35). ∎

Lemma 5.

Let the solutions αs=αs​(t,x)\alpha^{s}=\alpha^{s}(t,x) and βs=βs​(t,x)\beta^{s}=\beta^{s}(t,x) of the (backward) linear heat equation satisfy the additional condition αxs​βs−αs​βxs=0\alpha^{s}_{x}\beta^{s}-\alpha^{s}\beta^{s}_{x}=0. Then for any i,j∈ℕi,j\in{\mathbb{N}}

αis​βjs−αjs​βis=0.\alpha^{s}_{i}\beta^{s}_{j}-\alpha^{s}_{j}\beta^{s}_{i}=0. (36)

Hereafter the subscripts ii and jj denote the ii-th and jj-th order derivatives with respect to xx.

Proof.

We make the proof by means of mathematical induction with respect to the value i+ji+j.

Equation (36) is trivial for i+j=0i+j=0, coincides with the additional condition for i+j=1i+j=1 and is obtained from this condition by means of differentiation with respect to xx if i+j=2i+j=2.

Let us suppose that the Lemma’s statement is true if i+j=m−1i+j=m-1 and i+j=mi+j=m and prove it for i+j=m+1i+j=m+1. Acting on equation (36) where i+j=m−1i+j=m-1 with the operator ∂t+∂x​x\partial_{t}+\partial_{xx} and taking into account the conditions αts+αx​xs=0\alpha^{s}_{t}+\alpha^{s}_{xx}=0 and βts+βx​xs=0\beta^{s}_{t}+\beta^{s}_{xx}=0, we obtain the equation

αi+1s​βj+1s−αj+1s​βi+1s=0.\alpha^{s}_{i+1}\beta^{s}_{j+1}-\alpha^{s}_{j+1}\beta^{s}_{i+1}=0.

Therefore, the statement is true for i′+j′=m+1i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}=m+1, 1≤i′,j′≤m1\leq i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\leq m (i′=i+1i^{\prime}=i+1, j′=j+1j^{\prime}=j+1). It remains to perform the proof in the case i′=m+1i^{\prime}=m+1, j′=0j^{\prime}=0 (or equivalently i′=0i^{\prime}=0, j′=m+1j^{\prime}=m+1). For these values of i′i^{\prime} and j′j^{\prime} the statement is produced by subtracting the induced above equation αms​β1s−α1s​βms=0\alpha^{s}_{m}\beta^{s}_{1}-\alpha^{s}_{1}\beta^{s}_{m}=0 from the results of differentiation of equation (36) where i=mi=m, j=0j=0 with respect to xx. ∎

Let W⁡(φ1,…,φl)W(\varphi^{1},\ldots,\varphi^{l}) denotes the Wronskian of the functions φ1\varphi^{1}, …, φl\varphi^{l} with respect to the variable xx, i.e. W⁡(φ1,…,φl)=det(φij)i,j=1lW(\varphi^{1},\ldots,\varphi^{l})=\det(\varphi^{j}_{i})_{i,j=1}^{\;l}.

Lemma 6.

The solutions φ1=φ1​(t,x)\varphi^{1}=\varphi^{1}(t,x), …, φl=φl​(t,x)\varphi^{l}=\varphi^{l}(t,x) of a linear evolution equation L​φ=0L\varphi=0 are linear dependent iff W⁡(φ1,…,φl)=0W(\varphi^{1},\ldots,\varphi^{l})=0.

Proof.

Since the equation L​φ=0L\varphi=0 is linear and evolution the operator LL is the sum of ∂t\partial_{t} and linear differential operator with respect to xx with the coefficients depending on tt and xx. If the functions φ1\varphi^{1}, …, φl\varphi^{l} are linear dependent then the equality W⁡(φ1,…,φl)=0W(\varphi^{1},\ldots,\varphi^{l})=0 is obvious. Let us prove the inverse statement.

In the case l=2l=2 the condition W⁡(φ1,φ2)=0W(\varphi^{1},\varphi^{2})=0 implies φ2=C​φ1\varphi^{2}=C\varphi^{1}, where CC is a smooth function of tt. Acting on the latter equality with the operator LL, we obtain Ct​φ1=0C_{t}\varphi^{1}=0, i.e. C=constC=\mathop{\rm const}\nolimits or φ1=0\varphi^{1}=0. In any case the functions φ1\varphi^{1} and φ2\varphi^{2} are linear dependent.

Suppose W⁡(φ1,…,φl)=0W(\varphi^{1},\ldots,\varphi^{l})=0. Without loss of generality we can assume W⁡(φ1,…,φl−1)≠0W(\varphi^{1},\ldots,\varphi^{l-1})\neq 0. (Otherwise we consider a less value of ll.) Then φl=Ck​φk,\varphi^{l}=C^{k}\varphi^{k}, where CkC^{k} are smooth functions of tt and the superscript kk runs from 1 to l−1l-1. Action of the operator LL on the latter equality results in the equation Ctk​φk=0C^{k}_{t}\varphi^{k}=0 that implies, in view of the condition W⁡(φ1,…,φl−1)≠0W(\varphi^{1},\ldots,\varphi^{l-1})\neq 0, Ck=constC^{k}=\mathop{\rm const}\nolimits. It gives the Lemma’s statement. ∎

Lemma 7.

If αis​βjs−αjs​βis=0\alpha^{s}_{i}\beta^{s}_{j}-\alpha^{s}_{j}\beta^{s}_{i}=0 for 0≤i<j≤p0\leq i<j\leq p then W⁡(α1,…,αp,βs′)=0W(\alpha^{1},\ldots,\alpha^{p},\beta^{s^{\prime}})=0 for any s′s^{\prime}.

Proof.

Let Mi​js′M^{s^{\prime}}_{ij} denote the (p−1)(p-1)-th order minor of W⁡(α¯,βs′)W(\bar{\alpha},\beta^{s^{\prime}}), which is obtained by means of deletion of s′s^{\prime}-th and (p+1)(p+1)-th columns corresponding to the functions αs′\alpha^{s^{\prime}} and βs′\beta^{s^{\prime}} and ii-th and jj-th rows. Let us multiply the equation αis​βjs−αjs​βis=0\alpha^{s}_{i}\beta^{s}_{j}-\alpha^{s}_{j}\beta^{s}_{i}=0 by (−1)i+j+s′+p+1​Mi​js′(-1)^{i+j+s^{\prime}+p+1}M^{s^{\prime}}_{ij} and convolve with respect to the indices ii and jj. In view of the Laplace theorem on determinant expansion we obtain

W⁡(α¯|αs↝αs′,βs)=0.W(\bar{\alpha}|_{\alpha^{s}\rightsquigarrow\alpha^{s^{\prime}}},\beta^{s})=0.

Here the sign “↝\rightsquigarrow” means that the function αs\alpha^{s} is substituted instead of the function αs′\alpha^{s^{\prime}} and we have summation over the index ss. The Lemma’s statement easily follows from the latter equation since for any fixed s≠s′s\neq s^{\prime} we have W⁡(α¯|αs↝αs′,βs)=0W(\bar{\alpha}|_{\alpha^{s}\rightsquigarrow\alpha^{s^{\prime}}},\beta^{s})=0. ∎

Lemma 8.

The general solution of system (35) can be presented in the form

K=αs​Hvs+β0,K=\alpha^{s}H_{v^{s}}+\beta^{0}, (37)

where HH is an arbitrary smooth function of v¯\bar{v}, β0=β0​(t,x)\beta^{0}=\beta^{0}(t,x) is an arbitrary solution of the backward linear heat equation.

Proof.

In view of Lemma 4 the functions αs\alpha^{s} and βs=Kvs\beta^{s}=K_{v^{s}} satisfy the conditions of Lemma 5 and, therefore, the ones of Lemma 7, and the variables v¯\bar{v} are assumed as parameters. (αiσ​αjς−αjσ​αiς)​(Pvσς−Pvςσ)=0.(\alpha^{\sigma}_{i}\alpha^{\varsigma}_{j}-\alpha^{\sigma}_{j}\alpha^{\varsigma}_{i})(P^{\varsigma}_{v^{\sigma}}-P^{\sigma}_{v^{\varsigma}})=0. (38)

In view of Lemma 8 the conserved vector (K​u,Kx​u−K​ux)(Ku,K_{x}u-Ku_{x}) from Lemma 4 has the form (β0​u+Dx​H,βx0​u−β0​ux−Dt​H)(\beta^{0}u+D_{x}H,\beta^{0}_{x}u-\beta^{0}u_{x}-D_{t}H).

9 Potential conservation laws of
nonlinear diffusion–convection equations

More general potential conservation laws than simplest ones are admissible only if the investigated system has

  • •

    either more than one linear independent local conservation laws (and, therefore, we can introduce a number of different potentials for the first iteration step)

  • •

    or non-trivial simplest potential conservation laws.

As shown in Section 7, it is possible in class (1) only for special values of the parameter functions AA and BB. In view of results of Section 7 for the linearizable equations and Theorem 8, we can formulate the following statement.

Theorem 9.

For any linearizable equation from class (1) all potential conservation laws of the second level are equivalent on the manifold of the corresponding potential systems to potential conservation laws of the first level.

To investigate completely the potential conservation laws of equations from class (1), it remains to study the subclasses with B=0B=0 and B=AB=A, equations from which have two independent local conservation laws, and the subclass B=∫A+u​AB=\int\!A+uA reduced to B=AB=A by means of potential equivalence transformations.

Theorem 10.

All potential conservation laws of any equation from class (1) with B=0B=0 or B=AB=A are trivial on the manifold of the united potential systems (19), (20) and (23), (24) constructed with pairs of independent local conservation laws.

Proof.

Consider the united system (19), (20) (or (23), (24)). (Below we write down the differences of the second case with the first one in brackets.) Similarly to Lemma 3, we can assume without loss of generality that F=F⁡(t,x,v1,v2)F=F(t,x,v^{1},v^{2}) and G=G⁡(t,x,u,v1,v2)G=G(t,x,u,v^{1},v^{2}). Let us split the equation Dt​F+Dx​G=0D_{t}F+D_{x}G=0 on the manifold determining by the united system. Integration of one from the obtained equations results in the following expression for the flux GG: G=−(QF)∫A+G0,G=-(QF)\textstyle\int\!A+G^{0}, where G0=G0​(t,x,v1,v2)G^{0}=G^{0}(t,x,v^{1},v^{2}) and Q=∂v1+x∂v2Q=\partial_{v^{1}}+x\partial_{v^{2}} (Q=∂v1+ex∂v2Q=\partial_{v^{1}}+e^{x}\partial_{v^{2}}). The other equations form the system on the functions FF and G0G^{0}:

Q2F=0,QG0=0,Ft+Gx0=0,(QF)x+Fv2=0((QF)x−Fv1=0).Q^{2}F=0,\quad QG^{0}=0,\quad F_{t}+G^{0}_{x}=0,\quad(QF)_{x}+F_{v^{2}}=0\quad(\,(QF)_{x}-F_{v^{1}}=0\,).

Therefore, F=F1​v1+F0F=F^{1}v^{1}+F^{0}, and F1F^{1}, F0F^{0} and G0G^{0} are functions of tt, y=xy=x and ω=x​v1−v2\omega=xv^{1}-v^{2} (ω=ex​v1−v2\omega=e^{x}v^{1}-v^{2}) for which Fω0=Fy1F^{0}_{\omega}=F^{1}_{y}, Ft1=−Gω0F^{1}_{t}=-G^{0}_{\omega}, Ft0=−Gy0F^{0}_{t}=-G^{0}_{y}. The latter system implies existence of such function H=H⁡(t,y,ω)H=H(t,y,\omega) that

F1=Hω(F1=ex​Hω),F0=Hy,G0=−Ht.F^{1}=H_{\omega}\quad(F^{1}=e^{x}H_{\omega}),\quad F^{0}=H_{y},\quad G^{0}=-H_{t}.

Then, F=Dx​HF=D_{x}H, G=−Dt​HG=-D_{t}H, i.e. the conservation law is trivial. ∎

As shown above, there exists the following chain of local transformations between potential systems: 1.3 ⟷\longleftrightarrow 1.2 ⟷\longleftrightarrow (23), (24), i.e. system 1.3 is locally equivalent to system (23), (24). In view of this fact and Theorem 10 we obtain the following statement.

Theorem 11.

On the manifold of the potential system 1.3 all potential conservation laws of any equation from class (1) with B=∫A+u​AB=\int\!A+uA are trivial.

Summarizing the above results, we note that up to G∼G^{\mathop{\sim}}-equivalence the hierarchy of conservation laws (including local ones) for diffusion–convection equations (1) has the form:

  • •

    the “common” local conservation law (Case 1) for arbitrary values of the parameter functions AA and BB;

  • •

    two independent local conservation laws if B=0B=0 (Cases 1 and 2) or B=AB=A (Cases 1 and 3);

  • •

    one “common” local conservation law (Case 1) and one simplest potential that (Case 1.3) if B=∫A+u​AB=\int\!A+uA;

  • •

    the infinite series of local conservation laws (Case 4) for the linear heat equation;

  • •

    one “common” local conservation law (Case 1) and the infinite series of simplest potential conservation laws (Case 1.6) for the Burgers equation;

  • •

    two independent local conservation laws for the u−2u^{-2}-diffusion equation (Cases 1 and 2) and the equation ut=(u−2​ux)x+u−2​uxu_{t}=(u^{-2}u_{x})_{x}+u^{-2}u_{x} (Cases 1 and 3) as subcases of B=0B=0 and B=AB=A and the infinite series of simplest potential conservation laws (Cases 1.4 and 1.5) additionally.

Note 9.

Above we did not consider in an explicit form action of transformations from Lie symmetry groups on conservation laws of corresponding equations or potential systems. For the majority of cases this action is quite trivial. For example, we use translations with respect to xx to normalize the constant ε\varepsilon in Case 3. In Case 2 the same translations result in adding the “common” conservation law to the special one of this case.

A non-obvious connection between independent conservation laws can be established only for A=u−4/3A=u^{-4/3}, B=0B=0 (Case 1 and Case 2) by means of the transformation t~=t\tilde{t}=t, x~=1−x−1\tilde{x}=1-x^{-1}, u~=x3​u\tilde{u}=x^{3}u from the Lie symmetry group of the corresponding equation. This fact was first discovered in [23] in the framework of the “operator” approach. It should be mentioned that the values A=u−4/3A=u^{-4/3}, B=0B=0 give rise to the equation which distinguishes from non-linear diffusion–convection equations (1) by singular Lie symmetry properties.

The Lie symmetry group 𝒢−{\mathcal{G}}_{-} of the linear heat equation contains infinite dimensional normal subgroup 𝒢−0{\mathcal{G}}_{-}^{0} formed by the linear superposition transformations u~=u+f⁡(t,x)\tilde{u}=u+f(t,x), where f=f⁡(t,x)f=f(t,x) is an arbitrary solution of the same equation. Up to the equivalence relation, transformations from 𝒢−0{\mathcal{G}}_{-}^{0} act identically on the set of conservations laws of Case 4. Action of the finite dimensional factor group 𝒢−/𝒢−0{\mathcal{G}}_{-}/{\mathcal{G}}_{-}^{0} on this set induces the analogous factor group 𝒢+/𝒢+0{\mathcal{G}}_{+}/{\mathcal{G}}_{+}^{0} on the set of solutions of the backward linear heat equation, which is varied over by the parameter-function α\alpha.

The hierarchy of conservation laws generates the complete set of locally inequivalent potential systems for the class under consideration:

  • •

    “common” potential system (18) (Case 1);

  • •

    additional simplest potential systems (20) (Case 2) or (24) (Case 3) if B=0B=0 or B=AB=A correspondingly;

  • •

    second level potential systems (21) (Case 1.1) and (25) (Case 1.2) (which are really equivalent to the united potential systems of the first level) if B=0B=0 or B=AB=A correspondingly;

  • •

    system (34) with arbitrary number of locally independent potentials for the linear heat equation.

Potential symmetries arising for equations (1) from Cases 1 and 1.1 of Table 1 were studied by C. Sophocleous [36]. Complete investigation of the potential system (18) (Case 1) with the symmetry point of view was carried out in [34].

10 Conclusion

The notions and methods proposed in the paper are simple and effective tools for investigation of both local and pure potential conservation laws. They can be applied to a wide range of physically interesting systems of differential equations. At the same time, there exist a number of unresolved problems, in particular, on determining the number of necessary iterations for construction of an exhaustive list of independent potential conservation laws or on connections of our framework with Wahlquist–Estabrook prolongation structures [42].

The adduced results for diffusion–convection equations can be developed and generalized in a number of directions. So, studying different kinds of symmetries (Lie, nonclassical, generalized ones) of constructed potential systems, we may obtain the corresponding kinds of potential symmetries (usual potential, nonclassical potential, generalized potential ones). Let us note that investigation of generalized symmetries is natural for potential systems, since potentials introduced with equivalent conservation laws are related, in general, via transformations depending on derivatives of local dependent variables. Analogously, local equivalence transformations between potential systems constructed for different initial equations result in nonlocal (potential) equivalence transformations for the class under consideration. In such way it is possible to find new connections between well-studied diffusion–convection equations [34]. We believe that the same approach can be used for investigation of wider classes of differential equations, e.g. variable coefficient diffusion–convection equations. We also plan to study conservation laws of more general structure (e.g. ones with pseudopotentials).
